title: Problem Overview and References
content: Erdős Problem #815 asks whether 'degree 3 critical' graphs must contain cycles of all lengths $k \geq 3$. A degree 3 critical graph has $n$ vertices, $2n-2$ edges, and every proper induced subgraph has minimum degree $\leq 2$. The conjecture was posed by Erdős and Hajnal and DISPROVED by Narins, Pokrovskiy, and Szabó (2017), who constructed arbitrarily large such graphs avoiding $C_{23}$. Earlier, Erdős, Faudree, Gyárfás, and Schelp (1988) proved that $C_3$, $C_4$, $C_5$ always exist and that the longest cycle lies between $\log_2 n$ and $\sqrt{n}$.
mathContext: Does $G$ degree 3 critical with $|V| = n$, $|E| = 2n - 2$ imply $C_k \subseteq G$ for all $k \geq 3$? Answer: NO ($C_{23}$ can be avoided).

title: Imports and Setup
content: Imports Mathlib's simple graph infrastructure, subgraph module (for induced subgraphs), connectivity (for walk-based cycle definitions), and finite set cardinality. The variable `{V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]` makes all definitions polymorphic over the vertex type, which is crucial for the counterexample axiom that existentially quantifies over vertex types.
mathContext: Uses `SimpleGraph V`, `G.induce S` for induced subgraphs, `G.Walk v v` for cycles

title: Minimum Degree
content: `minDegree G` computes the smallest vertex degree using `Finset.min'` over the image of the degree function. This is noncomputable because `Finset.min'` uses classical logic to select the minimum. The minimum degree is the key parameter in the 'degree 3 critical' definition: the condition says all proper subgraphs have minimum degree $\leq 2$.

title: Degree 3 Critical Graphs
content: `IsDegree3Critical G` combines three conditions: (1) $|V| > 0$ (non-empty), (2) $|E| = 2|V| - 2$ (specific edge density), and (3) every proper induced subgraph on $S \subsetneq V$ has minimum degree $\leq 2$. The name 'degree 3 critical' reflects that these are minimal graphs where some vertex has degree $\geq 3$: the $2n - 2$ edge count gives average degree $\approx 4$, but the subgraph condition prevents this density from concentrating in any proper subgraph.

title: Cycles in Graphs
content: `HasCycleOfLength G k` asserts the existence of a closed trail (walk that doesn't repeat edges) of length $k \geq 3$ starting and ending at the same vertex. `ContainsCk` is a synonym. Using trails rather than simple paths is a simplification — for cycles in simple graphs, the two notions coincide when the cycle is the shortest closed walk through its vertices.
mathContext: $C_k \subseteq G \iff \exists$ closed trail of length $k \geq 3$ in $G$

title: The Erdős-Hajnal Conjecture
content: `ErdosHajnalConjecture` states: for all $k \geq 3$, there exists $N$ such that every degree 3 critical graph on $\geq N$ vertices contains $C_k$. This is a strong assertion — it would mean that the rich cycle structure of these graphs is *universal*, containing cycles of every possible length. The quantifier order ($\forall k, \exists N, \forall G$) allows $N$ to depend on $k$, which is the natural formulation for asymptotic graph theory.
mathContext: $\forall k \geq 3,\, \exists N,\, \forall G$ degree 3 critical with $|V| \geq N$: $C_k \subseteq G$

title: EFGS Short Cycles (1988): C₃, C₄, C₅ Always Exist
content: The axiom `efgs_short_cycles` captures the Erdős-Faudree-Gyárfás-Schelp theorem: every degree 3 critical graph on $n \geq 5$ vertices contains $C_3$, $C_4$, AND $C_5$. The proof for $C_3$ follows from the edge density ($2n - 2$ edges forces triangles for large $n$ by Turán-type arguments). The $C_4$ and $C_5$ proofs require more delicate structural analysis of the degree 3 critical condition.

title: EFGS Cycle Length Bounds: log₂(n) to √n
content: Two axioms capture the EFGS bounds on the longest cycle. `efgs_long_cycle`: every degree 3 critical graph contains a cycle of length $\geq \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, providing a guaranteed minimum. `efgs_upper_bound`: there exist degree 3 critical graphs whose longest cycle has length $\leq \sqrt{n}$, showing the longest cycle can be much shorter than $n$. The gap between $\log_2 n$ and $\sqrt{n}$ represents the range of possible longest cycle lengths.
mathContext: $\log_2 n \leq \max\{k : C_k \subseteq G\} \leq \sqrt{n}$ for degree 3 critical $G$ on $n$ vertices

title: Erdős-Hajnal Partial Result: k = 3, 4, 5, 6
content: `erdos_hajnal_small_k` states that the conjecture holds for $3 \leq k \leq 6$: degree 3 critical graphs always contain $C_k$ for these values. The cases $k = 3, 4, 5$ follow from `efgs_short_cycles`. The case $k = 6$ was claimed by Erdős and Hajnal but is left as `sorry` — it would require a separate proof or axiom. This is the one remaining sorry in the file.
mathContext: $3 \leq k \leq 6 \Rightarrow \exists N,\, \forall G$ degree 3 critical with $|V| \geq N$: $C_k \subseteq G$

title: Narins-Pokrovskiy-Szabó Counterexample (2017)
content: The axiom `narins_pokrovskiy_szabo` formalizes the breakthrough counterexample: for any $N$, there exists a degree 3 critical graph on $\geq N$ vertices with no $C_{23}$. The number 23 is the smallest odd $k$ where their recursive construction technique works. The construction builds graphs satisfying $|E| = 2|V| - 2$ and the subgraph condition while carefully avoiding any 23-cycle, using graph products and local cycle analysis.
mathContext: $\forall N,\, \exists G$ degree 3 critical with $|V| \geq N$ and $C_{23} \not\subseteq G$

title: Formal Disproof: erdos_815_disproved
content: The theorem `erdos_815_disproved` proves $\neg\text{ErdosHajnalConjecture}$ by contradiction. Assuming the conjecture, specialize to $k = 23$ to get $N$ such that all large degree 3 critical graphs contain $C_{23}$. Then `narins_pokrovskiy_szabo` provides a graph on $\geq N$ vertices that IS degree 3 critical but does NOT contain $C_{23}$. The contradiction is extracted by `exact hno23 (hN V G hcard hcrit)`. This is a clean, 4-line proof.
mathContext: $\text{ErdosHajnalConj} \Rightarrow (\exists N,\, \forall |V| \geq N: C_{23} \subseteq G) \wedge (\exists G: |V| \geq N \wedge C_{23} \not\subseteq G) \Rightarrow \bot$

title: Open Problem: Even k Conjecture
content: `evenKConjecture` formalizes the remaining open question: does every degree 3 critical graph contain $C_k$ for all even $k \geq 4$? The Narins-Pokrovskiy-Szabó counterexample uses $k = 23$ (odd), and their technique specifically exploits odd cycle structure. Even and odd cycles behave differently in graph theory (e.g., bipartite graphs have no odd cycles), so the even case may require entirely different techniques.
mathContext: $\forall k \geq 4$ even: $\exists N,\, \forall G$ degree 3 critical with $|V| \geq N$: $C_k \subseteq G$? (OPEN)

title: Motivation and Construction Idea
content: Two expository sections explain: (1) Why 'degree 3 critical'? The $2n-2$ edge count gives average degree $\approx 4$, but the subgraph condition prevents any proper subgraph from having minimum degree $\geq 3$. These graphs are minimal witnesses to having a vertex of degree $\geq 3$. (2) How the counterexample works: Narins-Pokrovskiy-Szabó use recursive structure, graph products, and local cycle analysis. The choice of 23 is the smallest odd $k$ where their technique succeeds.
mathContext: Average degree $= 2|E|/|V| = 2(2n-2)/n \approx 4$; subgraph condition prevents dense cores

title: Summary Theorem: erdos_815_summary
content: The summary theorem `erdos_815_summary` packages two results: (1) $\neg\text{ErdosHajnalConjecture}$ (the disproof), and (2) the EFGS positive result that degree 3 critical graphs on $\geq 5$ vertices always contain $C_3$, $C_4$, $C_5$. The proof constructs the pair directly from `erdos_815_disproved` and `efgs_short_cycles`. This captures the full picture: the conjecture fails globally ($C_{23}$ can be avoided) but succeeds locally (short cycles are forced).
